1016.title: The bathhouse
1016.hook: public baths near mosques, for cleanliness and community
1016.howItsDone: Muslims make wudu before prayer and ghusl after major impurity and, by custom, before Friday prayer; historic hammams are still in use in cities such as Istanbul, Fez, Cairo and Damascus, with separate hours or sections for men and women.

segments.voice: Yesterday: caravanserais and khans, road houses that made a stranger a guest: rest for the traveler.

Steam, first. Then the sounds: water poured from a metal bowl onto stone, voices echoing under a low dome pierced with small round windows of glass, so the light comes down in coins. Someone is scrubbing someone else's back. Someone is lying on a warm marble slab, staring up at the coins of light. Outside, a few steps away, the market is loud and the mosque is waiting for the next prayer. Today: the bathhouse. The word is hammam.
screen: `STEAM AND ECHOES.` → `LIGHT FALLING IN COINS.` → `BETWEEN MARKET AND MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Washing sits close to the heart of Muslim practice. Before prayer comes wudu: washing the face, the hands and arms, wiping the head, and then the feet, as surah five of the Qur'an sets out. Sunni Muslims wash the feet; Shia Muslims read the same verse as asking them to wipe. After certain states, such as sex or menstruation, comes ghusl, a full bath. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih Muslim calls purity half of faith. Another, in Sahih al-Bukhari, asks those coming to Friday prayer to bathe first. And the Qur'an says that God loves those who turn to Him, and loves those who keep themselves clean. So in a town where houses had no running water, a public bath wasn't a luxury. It was where the town got ready to pray. Hammams were built near mosques and markets. Some were endowed as waqf, and their fees helped pay for the mosque or school next door. Inside, a path from cool to warm to hot, and back again. Men and women went at separate hours or to separate baths. And the hammam was more than washing. Neighbors met there. Before a wedding, or after a birth, families came with food and music. People also tell of mothers looking over the young women at the baths for a bride for their sons. There were limits too: a hadith collected by al-Tirmidhi tells men to enter only with a waist cloth. The hammam held both: strict about the body, generous with company. Clean together.
screen: `WUDU, GHUSL, HALF OF FAITH.` · `A TOWN GETTING READY TO PRAY.` · `COOL, WARM, HOT, AND BACK.` · `STRICT ABOUT BODIES, GENEROUS WITH COMPANY.` · then, large: `CLEAN TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Wash your hands and face slowly now, or simply imagine it, and feel the water's temperature: the hands, then the face, then the back of the neck, where it feels cool and where it warms. If you pray, you can make it your wudu, with intention; if you don't, let it be a slow, careful wash.
Hammam. The public bathhouse near the mosque and the market, for cleanliness and for company. Today's word.
Your line: clean together. A town getting ready to pray, side by side. See you tomorrow.

1017.title: The soup kitchen
1017.hook: Ottoman imarets fed the poor daily
1017.howItsDone: Mosques and Muslim charities often run community kitchens and food drives, especially in Ramadan, when meals to break the fast are often shared freely with anyone who comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hammam, the bathhouse near the mosque, where a town got clean side by side. Your line was clean together.

A row of great copper pots, already bubbling before the sun is fully up. A cook stirs with a ladle as long as an arm. Outside the door a line is forming: a student with a bowl, an old widow, a traveler still dusty from the road, a man who has not eaten since yesterday. Nobody asks for a coin, or a name. The bowls go out full, and the cooks start the next pot. This isn't a story about one kind neighbor. It's about a building made to do this every day, whether anyone felt generous that morning or not. Today: the soup kitchen.
screen: `COPPER POTS BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `A LINE AT THE DOOR.` → `NOBODY ASKS FOR A COIN.`

segments.voice: The Ottomans called it an imaret. Often it stood beside a mosque, inside a larger complex that might also hold a school, a guest house, sometimes a hospital. The food came from the idea we met a few days ago, the waqf, the endowment. Someone with means gave land or shops or rents forever, and the income paid for bread and soup, cooks and firewood, long after the giver was gone. So the meal at the door didn't depend on anyone's mood. It was written into the deed. Who ate? The deeds that survive set out the order, and it varied from place to place: students and teachers, travelers, the poor of the neighborhood, the staff themselves. Historians read them closely, because they show charity planned like a kitchen schedule. Why build such a thing? The Qur'an describes the righteous this way, in Pickthall's words: "And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him, (Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." No reward. Not even thanks. The bowl is not a trade. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari to have told people to feed the hungry, visit the sick, and set captives free: one plain instruction in a short list. The imaret gave that line a roof, a chimney, and a budget, a promise kept in public. Soup for all.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who could use a meal: a neighbor who has been ill, a friend with a new baby, a coworker who skips lunch, or a stranger you'll never meet, through a food bank. Picture the bowl or the bag of groceries reaching them, with nothing asked back. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if not, just keep their face in mind and breathe.
Imaret. The Ottoman kitchen beside the mosque, paid for by an endowment so the bowls went out every day. Today's word.
Your line: soup for all. A full bowl, and not even thanks expected. I'll keep a seat for you.

1018.title: The libraries
1018.hook: from Cordoba to Cairo to Timbuktu, great libraries
1018.howItsDone: Muslims often treat books of religious learning with care, keeping copies of the Qur'an on a high shelf, and mosques often keep a small library for study and teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the imaret, the soup kitchen beside the mosque, paid for so the bowls kept going out. Your line was soup for all.

A family in Timbuktu opens a wooden chest. Inside, wrapped in cloth and leather, are pages written by hand: prayers, law, astronomy, letters, poems, notes in the margins from readers long dead. Families in that desert city kept papers like these for generations, and when they were threatened, people carried them away to safety. Why risk that much for old paper? Because, to those families, a book was more than an object. In city after city across the Muslim world, people built rooms for books and opened their doors. Today: the libraries.
screen: `A CHEST OPENS IN TIMBUKTU.` → `PAGES CARRIED TO SAFETY.` → `WHY RISK IT FOR PAPER?`

segments.voice: Start with an oath. One surah of the Qur'an opens by swearing on writing itself. In Pickthall's translation: "By the pen and that which they write." Now walk the map. In Cordoba, in Muslim Spain, the court of the caliphs gathered a royal library, and chroniclers wrote of its size with open wonder. In Cairo, the Fatimid rulers founded a house of knowledge, Dar al-Ilm, where people could come to read, copy and study. In Timbuktu, the books lived not only in one great hall but in mosques, schools and family homes, passed down hand to hand. Three cities, three shapes of the same habit. What filled the shelves? The Qur'an and its commentaries, law and hadith, yes. But also medicine, mathematics, grammar, poetry, geography, the stars. Some collections were endowed through a waqf, like yesterday's soup kitchen, so the books stayed open to readers rather than locked away. Some of these libraries burned, were scattered in wars, or were sold off page by page; some survive in pieces in archives around the world. What lasted longest was the expectation itself: that a city worth the name kept its books, and let people read them. A library in every city.
screen: `AN OATH BY THE PEN.` · `CORDOBA: THE CALIPHS' LIBRARY.` · `CAIRO: THE HOUSE OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `TIMBUKTU: BOOKS IN FAMILY HOMES.` · then, large: `BY THE PEN AND THAT WHICH THEY WRITE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've always been curious about and never looked into: a place, a craft, a stretch of history, a question about the stars. Picture the library shelf and the book that could answer it, kept by someone so a stranger could read it for free. If you pray, ask to learn something good; if not, just stay curious and breathe.
The libraries. From Cordoba to Cairo to Timbuktu, rooms of books, often endowed, kept open for readers. Today's word.
Your line: a library in every city. Every open shelf was someone's gift to a stranger. Day one thousand eighteen, done.

1019.title: Colonial rule
1019.hook: from the 1700s to the 1900s, much of the Muslim world came under European rule
1019.howItsDone: Muslim communities remember the colonial period in many ways, from national holidays and museums to the stories of grandparents, and Muslim historians and scholars continue to debate how it changed religious life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the libraries, rooms of books kept open for readers. Your line was a library in every city. Today, a harder turn.

A school map, the kind that once hung on classroom walls, shaded in a few colors, one for each European empire. Now lay a second map over it: where Muslims lived. From North Africa to the Indian Ocean, from West Africa to the islands of Southeast Asia, much of it sits under the colors of the first. Behind every patch are real towns, mosques and families, ruled within a lifetime by people from far away. That's a lot for one lesson, so this one is about one thing: how to tell it. Today: colonial rule.
screen: `A CLASSROOM MAP, SHADED IN COLORS.` → `LAY THE MUSLIM WORLD OVER IT.` → `TODAY: HOW TO TELL IT.`

segments.voice: Over the modern centuries, European powers came to rule a great deal of the Muslim world. The British in India and Egypt. The French in Algeria. The Dutch in the islands we now call Indonesia. The stories differ from place to place, and an honest telling keeps them different. Some of what came was conquest, war and land taken. Some was railways, telegraph lines and schools, built mostly to serve the rulers and later put to use by the ruled. Borders were drawn by people who would never live inside them. Old institutions, like the endowments we've been meeting, were in some places taken over or redirected. Muslims answered in many ways, and they didn't agree with each other. Some took up arms. Some opened new schools. Some worked inside the colonial system and tried to soften it. Some went into exile. One life refuses a simple telling. Emir Abdelkader led years of armed resistance to the French in Algeria, lost, and was eventually exiled. Later, living in Damascus, he saw mobs turn on the city's Christians, and he and his men sheltered many of them. A fighter against a European empire, protecting Christians from a Muslim mob. Both true. The Qur'an asks for this honesty. In Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Justice even against your own side. So name the harm plainly, name those who resisted and those who didn't, and leave nobody out because they spoil the story. Told honestly.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one Muslim-majority country, maybe your family's, maybe one you know only from the news. Hold three plain questions beside it: who ruled it, and from where; what did people lose; who resisted, and how? If you pray, remember its people; if not, let the place stay in mind as you breathe.
Colonial rule. The long stretch when European empires ruled much of the Muslim world, a history to be told with justice, even when it's uncomfortable. Today's word.
Your line: told honestly. The hard parts and the brave parts both belong. Rest easy until tomorrow.

1020.title: The last Mughal, 1857
1020.hook: the last Mughal emperor is exiled after the uprising in India
1020.howItsDone: Visitors still come to Bahadur Shah Zafar's tomb in Yangon to pray and to recite his poetry, and his ghazals are sung in Urdu across South Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday: colonial rule, and how to tell it, with justice even against your own side. Your line was told honestly. Today, one place, one year, one old man.

An elderly emperor sits in the Red Fort in Delhi, writing poetry. He rules very little beyond its walls; the British East India Company holds the real power. Then soldiers in the Company's own army rise up, march on Delhi, and call on him to lead them. He hesitates, then lends them his name. For a few months the old poet is again the center of an empire's hopes. When the British retake the city, he is put on trial and sent far away, across the sea. A dynasty that ruled for generations ends with an old man on a ship. Today: the last Mughal.
screen: `AN OLD EMPEROR WRITING POETRY.` → `THE SOLDIERS RISE.` → `AN EMPIRE ENDS ON A SHIP.`

segments.voice: His name was Bahadur Shah, and he wrote under the pen name Zafar, which means victory. A man called victory, remembered for a defeat. The Mughals had built the Taj Mahal and ruled much of South Asia; by Zafar's time, their power was mostly ceremony. Then came the uprising the British called a mutiny, and that others in India later called a war of independence. Even the name is still argued over, and an honest telling says so. The rising failed. Delhi was retaken, and the reprisals were brutal. Some of the emperor's sons were killed. Zafar was tried, found guilty, and exiled to Rangoon, in what is now Myanmar, where he died far from home. Now the poet's part. A couplet often attributed to him laments that the unlucky Zafar could not find even two yards of earth for his grave in the lane of the beloved. Scholars debate whether he wrote it. People keep reciting it anyway, because it says what his life became: a king who couldn't choose his own grave. How does the Qur'an speak of endings like this? In surah ar-Rahman, in Pickthall's words: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory." Every throne, every dynasty, every poet. What lasts, the verse says, is not ours. The crown was taken. The ghazals he wrote are still sung. The last emperor.
screen: `ZAFAR: A KING CALLED VICTORY.` · `A RISING WITH TWO NAMES.` · `EXILED TO RANGOON.` · `TWO YARDS OF EARTH.` · then, large: `THERE REMAINETH BUT THE COUNTENANCE OF THY LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that has ended or is ending: a job, a home, a friendship, a version of yourself. Don't fix it or argue with it; look at it like an old photograph, and notice what you carried out of it. If you pray, you can say the words of Qur'an 55, that everyone passes and the Countenance of the Lord remains; if not, just breathe with what has ended.

Your line: the last emperor. A crown can be taken while a song keeps going. That's day one thousand twenty.

1021.title: The reformers
1021.hook: thinkers like Jamal al-Din al-Afghani and Muhammad Abduh call for renewal and education
1021.howItsDone: Muslims today debate the reformers' legacy in universities, mosques and journals; some schools and movements trace their approach to Abduh's emphasis on education, while others follow older scholarly methods more closely.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zafar, the last Mughal, the poet emperor exiled across the sea. Your line was the last emperor. Today, people who refused to let an ending be the end.

Why are our lands ruled by others? A restless teacher with a sharp tongue puts that question to a crowded room in Cairo: lamplight, glasses of tea, students leaning in. Then more. What have we forgotten? What would the Qur'an say about a world of steamships and newspapers? The teacher is Jamal al-Din, called al-Afghani. One of the students listening hardest is an Egyptian named Muhammad Abduh. Neither knows yet that their conversations will shape arguments Muslims are still having. Today: the reformers.
screen: `A CROWDED ROOM IN CAIRO.` → `WHY ARE WE RULED BY OTHERS?` → `A TEACHER AND A STUDENT.`

segments.voice: Start with the teacher. Al-Afghani moved from country to country; even where he was born is debated. Wherever he went, he urged Muslims to wake up, unite, and stand against foreign rule. For a time he and Abduh published a journal together in Paris, sending its pages back to Muslim readers. Then the student. Abduh grew calmer than his teacher, and came to believe the way forward ran through schools more than politics. He worked to reform teaching, including at al-Azhar, the great mosque university of Cairo, and late in life he served as Mufti of Egypt. His central conviction: reason and revelation do not fight. Read the Qur'an with an open mind, learn the sciences, and stop treating every inherited opinion as untouchable. The reformers often quoted one line of the Qur'an. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts." Change starts inside. They also leaned on a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud: that God will send this community, at the head of every hundred years, someone who renews its religion. Renewal, in this reading, is not a betrayal of tradition; it's part of the tradition's own promise. Not everyone agrees on what they started. Some Muslims honor them as renewers who opened the door to modern education. Others say they loosened the careful methods of the old scholars too quickly. Later movements, pulling in very different directions, have claimed them. That argument is part of their legacy. The word they kept returning to was renewal.
screen: `AL-AFGHANI: WAKE UP, UNITE.` · `ABDUH: REFORM THE SCHOOLS.` · `REASON AND REVELATION DON'T FIGHT.` · `A RENEWER, AT THE HEAD OF EVERY CENTURY.` · then, large: `CHANGE THAT WHICH IS IN THEIR HEARTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one part of your life that has gone stale: a habit kept out of routine, a prayer said without attention, a friendship you only maintain. Don't throw it out; ask what it was for in the first place, and what returning to that would look like. If you pray, hold Qur'an 13:11 in mind, that change begins in the heart; if not, let the question sit with your breathing.

1022.title: Muhammad Iqbal
1022.hook: the poet-philosopher of South Asia who urged the self to rise
1022.howItsDone: Iqbal's poems are recited and sung in Urdu and Persian at gatherings, in schools and in qawwali, and his lines are often quoted in sermons and speeches across South Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the reformers, al-Afghani and Abduh, calling for renewal through schools and reason. Your line was renewal. Today, renewal written as poetry.

A schoolyard in India. Children line up in the morning and sing a song that begins, in Urdu, with the claim that their land is better than all the world. A wedding in Lahore, and someone recites a couplet about the falcon who refuses to build a nest. A seminar room, and a professor lectures on how the Qur'an speaks of the human self. Three places, three audiences, one author: a poet who studied law and philosophy, wrote poetry in two languages, and kept asking what a human being is capable of. Today: Muhammad Iqbal.
screen: `A SONG IN A SCHOOLYARD.` → `A FALCON AT A WEDDING.` → `ONE POET BEHIND THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: Iqbal grew up in the Punjab, studied in Lahore, then in England and Germany. He came home a philosopher, a lawyer, and above all a poet, writing in Urdu and Persian. His great word was khudi: selfhood, the self. Not selfishness. For Iqbal, khudi was the spark God placed in each person, meant to be strengthened, not dissolved. He looked at Muslims under colonial rule and saw people who had learned to make themselves small: waiting, imitating, apologizing. His poetry kept saying the opposite. Rise. One often-quoted couplet goes, in paraphrase: raise your selfhood so high that, before each turn of destiny, God himself asks the servant, tell me, what do you wish? Bold words, meant boldly. But the self he praised is not a self without God. It grows strong by drawing near to God, the way a flame grows by being fed. A bird he returns to again and again is the falcon, a creature of the high air that, in his verse, won't settle for an easy nest. Behind this stands a line of surah at-Tin, in Pickthall's words: "Surely We created man of the best stature." Some readers hear Iqbal's idea in it: a dignity to grow into. Readers disagree about him, too. Some hear a poet of spiritual courage. Others focus on his politics, or argue over how far his philosophy strays from the old scholars. Pakistan honors him, and his songs are still sung in India. The self can rise.
screen: `A POET IN URDU AND PERSIAN.` · `KHUDI: SELFHOOD, NOT SELFISHNESS.` · `GOD ASKS: WHAT DO YOU WISH?` · `THE FALCON WON'T SETTLE.` · then, large: `SURELY WE CREATED MAN OF THE BEST STATURE.`

segments.voice: If there's a place in your life where you make yourself small, waiting for permission or apologizing for taking up room, bring it to mind. Ask what rising would look like there, not shouting, just standing a little taller, and let one true, hopeful sentence form. If you pray, hold the words of surah at-Tin, of the best stature; if not, just hold your line.
